people-are-meaner.name: Meanness
people-are-meaner.line: I see people treat each other meaner than they used to.
people-are-meaner.why: The ID names people getting meaner, but the wording drifted to an abstract 'moral decline'; this says what someone actually notices day to day and fits a problem-style heading.

people-are-meaner.name: Moral decline
people-are-meaner.line: I think people care less about treating each other decently.
people-are-meaner.why: Keeps the founder's 'moral decline' framing but grounds it in how people treat each other, which is what someone would say out loud, rather than 'right and wrong'.

trust.name: Distrust
trust.line: I can't trust the people around me any more.
trust.why: Drops 'and groups' so the pain is about everyday people, leaving institutions to the government heading, and 'Distrust' makes the name a problem like the rest of the heading.

nobody-knows-anybody.name: Strangers nearby
nobody-knows-anybody.line: I don't know the people on my street.
nobody-knows-anybody.why: Same line; 'Neighbors' is an area label in a heading of problem labels, while 'Strangers nearby' names the problem.

cant-pool.name: Can't pool money
cant-pool.line: I know we could afford it together, but there's no way to pool our money.
cant-pool.why: 'Sharing' is an area label and vague on its own; this names the problem and says what is being pooled.

town-dying.name: Dying town
town-dying.line: I'm watching my town empty out.
town-dying.why: 'Decline' alone could sit under many headings; 'Dying town' says what is declining and matches the ID.

building-cant-organize.name: Can't organize
building-cant-organize.line: I can't get my neighbors to act together on anything.
building-cant-organize.why: Makes the name a problem like the rest of the heading and keeps the plain everyday line.

pairs.distinction: Homelessness is seeing neighbors with no home; High rent is my own housing costing too much.
pairs.reason: One is about what I see happening to others and the other is about my own bills, so people can tell them apart at a glance.
Fearing I'll lose my own home is a personal pain, while seeing more neighbors with no home is a societal one, and the two are worth linking across pages.

pairs.distinction: Dying town is people and businesses leaving; Neighbors is not knowing the people who are still here.
pairs.reason: A town can be thriving and still full of strangers, so these are different complaints.

pairs.distinction: Dying town is the place emptying out; Local control is who makes the decisions about it.
pairs.reason: Someone watching their town empty out and someone angry that decisions are made elsewhere would each pick their own without hesitation.

pairs.distinction: Loneliness is feeling alone; Neighbors is not knowing the people on my street, which many people with close friends also feel.
pairs.reason: Not knowing neighbors is about the street and the community, while loneliness is a personal feeling that can happen anywhere.

pairs.distinction: Trust is whether I can rely on people around me; Moral decline is a sense that people treat each other worse.
pairs.reason: These are close, so the alternative wordings sharpen Trust toward relying on people and Moral decline toward how people treat each other.

pairs.distinction: Trust is about the people around me; Institutions is about courts, elections and agencies falling apart.
pairs.reason: The current Trust line says 'people and groups', which blurs into institutions, so the alternative drops 'groups' and keeps the two distinct.

pairs.distinction: Polarization is losing people when we disagree; Moral decline is people treating each other worse in general.
pairs.reason: Losing a friend over a disagreement is a specific experience that someone would pick out from a general sense that people are worse.

pairs.distinction: Sharing is wanting a way to pool money with others; Inequality is the gap between rich and poor growing.
pairs.reason: One is a missing tool for people to buy things together and the other is a society-wide gap, so they don't compete for the same pick.

pairs.distinction: Organizing is not getting neighbors to act at all; Meetings is groups that meet but get nothing done.
pairs.reason: Not being able to get anyone together and being stuck in meetings that go nowhere are different stages of the same effort, and people know which one they're in.

pairs.distinction: Housing is living somewhere cramped, broken or noisy; Organizing is not getting neighbors to act together.
pairs.reason: A bad apartment can be one reason to organize, but the pains are different and someone would not confuse them.

dirty-air.name: Dirty air
dirty-air.line: The air where I live isn't clean enough to breathe safely.
dirty-air.why: Brings the wording back to what the ID names and says the harm in words a neighbor would use, instead of the abstract "pollution harming".

dirty-air.name: Pollution
dirty-air.line: I worry the air and water where I live aren't safe.
dirty-air.why: Keeps the original name and its wider reach (water as well as air) while saying what is actually polluted, so the line is concrete enough to recognize.

car-or-nothing.name: Needing a car
car-or-nothing.line: I can't get anywhere without a car.
car-or-nothing.why: Same line; the name becomes a problem label like the rest of Environment (Climate change, Disasters, Pollution), so the heading no longer mixes styles.

nature-disappearing.name: Losing nature
nature-disappearing.line: I see fewer birds, trees and green spaces around me.
nature-disappearing.why: Turns the area label "Nature" into a problem label that matches the heading, and grounds the line in the person's own surroundings.

nature-disappearing.name: Disappearing wildlife
nature-disappearing.line: I see fewer birds, insects and wild places than I used to.
nature-disappearing.why: Names the loss over time that the ID points at, which separates it more clearly from climate change.

pairs.distinction: Climate change is the planet heating up over decades; dirty air is what I breathe in my own neighborhood today.
pairs.reason: Someone near a highway or a refinery and someone worried about global heating are naming different things, even when the same fuel causes both.

pairs.distinction: Disasters are floods, fires, storms and heat I'm living through now; climate change is the worry about where the planet is heading.
pairs.reason: A person rebuilding after a flood and a person anxious about the future would each pick one without thinking twice.

pairs.distinction: Losing nature is fewer birds, trees and green spaces near me, often from building and paving; climate change is global heating.
pairs.reason: Most nature loss people notice comes from development rather than heat, so the two point to different fixes.

pairs.distinction: On the personal page, getting around is my own trouble reaching places; on the societal page, needing a car is how towns are built.
pairs.reason: The same struggle shows up as a personal problem and as a design of places, so it belongs on both pages as two linked pains.

pairs.distinction: Infrastructure is roads, water and power breaking down; needing a car is having no other way to travel even when the roads work.
pairs.reason: Potholes and a missing bus line are different complaints, and a person would know which one they mean.

pairs.distinction: Kids' future is the fear that the next generation will have it worse for many reasons; climate change is one specific reason.
pairs.reason: Climate is one of several worries behind a fear for kids' future, so folding them together would lose both.

it-all-goes-up.name: Wealth gap
it-all-goes-up.line: I see a few people get richer every year while most of us fall further behind.
it-all-goes-up.why: Keeps the growing gap but says which way it moves, which is what the ID (everything goes up to the top) named; "Wealth gap" is plainer than "Inequality" and says gap in what.

justice-unfair.name: Unequal justice
justice-unfair.line: I see police and courts treat some people far worse than others for the same thing.
justice-unfair.why: "Justice" alone is an area label in a heading of problem labels; "for the same thing" says what unequal means without naming a group.

where-youre-born.name: Unequal chances
where-youre-born.line: I see kids born in some neighborhoods get far fewer chances than kids born a few miles away.
where-youre-born.why: "Opportunity" is an area label among problem labels; the line keeps the zip-code idea and makes it something you can picture.

where-youre-born.name: Unfair start
where-youre-born.line: I see where someone is born decide how their whole life turns out.
where-youre-born.why: Closest to the current line, with "where you're born decide your life" made into a full, natural sentence.

treated-differently.name: Discrimination against me
treated-differently.line: I get treated worse at work, in stores or by landlords because of who I am.
treated-differently.why: Says plainly that it happens to me, and where, so it can't be confused with watching it happen to others (Prejudice).

people-treated-badly.name: Prejudice around me
people-treated-badly.line: I see people around me treated badly because of their race, religion, or who they love.
people-treated-badly.why: "Discrimination" and "Prejudice" read as synonyms side by side; saying "around me" and naming common reasons makes this the one about others.

pairs.distinction: Discrimination is being treated worse myself; prejudice is seeing it happen to other people.
pairs.reason: Being on the receiving end and being a witness are different places to stand, but with the names "Discrimination" and "Prejudice" people can't tell them apart, so the alternatives sharpen both names.

pairs.distinction: Justice is unequal treatment by police and courts; prejudice is unequal treatment by people in everyday life.
pairs.reason: Someone angry about sentencing or policing names an institution, while someone bothered by how neighbors or coworkers treat people names something else, so each picks one easily.

pairs.distinction: Inequality is the gap in money and wealth now; opportunity is whether where you start decides where you end up.
pairs.reason: They often travel together, but someone can be bothered by the wealth gap today without naming mobility, and the other way around.

pairs.distinction: Rising prices squeeze my own budget; inequality is the gap between groups, which can grow even when prices are steady.
pairs.reason: Someone hit by prices and someone angry about the rich pulling away are naming different things, and either could pick one without the other.
Being shut out of places and services because of a disability is one personal form of being treated worse for who you are, so the two stay linked across pages.

pairs.distinction: Opportunity is some kids starting far behind others now; kids' future is a worry that this whole generation will have it worse than the last.
pairs.reason: One is a gap between kids and the other is a fall between generations, so a person can tell at once which one they mean.

Overlaps for review: water-pollution with dirty-air (Pollution) and the home sweep's tap-water candidate (personal view of the same worry); toxic-chemicals with dirty-air; noise with home-is-hard (Housing names noisy homes); water-shortages with disasters (drought) and infrastructure; trash-and-plastic with dirty-air. water-shortages and noise rest on European figures only; noise is weaker as a societal worry (8% in Eurobarometer) but common as exposure.
